clue.text: The limit starts to need adjustment in principle

indicators.note: letters that need adjustment are not yet in their right order
the rearranged letters sit in the word for principle

blocks.note: a law is a principle, as in a law of nature

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling that their patience has run out once a principle starts needing adjustment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' looks like a first-letters indicator; here it is the word to rearrange, and the result is packed between L and AW.
explanation.definitionFit: The last straw is the final thing that makes something intolerable, the limit of what can be borne.

clue.text: See 6
Overcoat or tutus for tailoring

indicators.note: cloth sent for tailoring is cut and re-sewn into a new shape

explanation.surface: A tailor's order book: an overcoat or some ballet tutus waiting to be made up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface stays in the tailor's shop, so the anagram indicator hides as ordinary dressmaking talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A surtout is a man's long close-fitting overcoat, from French for 'over all'.

clue.text: See 22 Across
Rap artist thanks junk

blocks.note: RA = Royal Academician, a standard artist

explanation.surface: A put-down of a rapper: the artist is thanked, and the music is junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rap artist' reads as one unit, a musician; split it and 'Rap' is the definition while 'artist' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A rap is a sharp knock, and rat-a-tat is the sound of knocking at a door.

clue.text: Cocktail: fancy drinking the blue one shortly

indicators.note: the fancy takes the blue in, as a drinker takes in a drink
'one' cut short loses its final letter

blocks.note: the blue = the sky, as in 'out of the blue'
an ace is a one on a playing card

explanation.surface: Someone ordering a cocktail and taking a fancy to the blue one on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an anagram indicator but is a noun here, a passing desire; 'the blue' is the poetic name for the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: A whisky mac is a mixed drink of Scotch whisky and ginger wine.

clue.text: Father of poetry?

blocks.note: the surface reads 'founder'; really a church title, the Holy Father
this father belongs to poetry: an 18th-century English poet shares the title as his surname

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as the founder of poetry; read 'Father' as the head of the Catholic Church, and Alexander Pope the poet shares his title.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Pope was a great English poet, and a pope is a Holy Father.

clue.text: 26 19's kind of wire in sensitive area

indicators.note: the wire sits in the sensitive area

blocks.note: a live wire is one carrying current

explanation.surface: A warning about a live wire running somewhere delicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 19 is NOEL COWARD, so the definition is one of his works; the answer runs on into 1 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Lives is Noel Coward's 1930 comedy of a divorced couple who meet again on honeymoon with new spouses.

clue.text: Inferior versifier, one sampling American author?

blocks.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer
a taster is one who samples

explanation.surface: A bad poet described as someone merely dipping into an American writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the answer is read two ways: the word itself, and POE plus TASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is a writer of trivial or inferior verse.

clue.text: With last of goulash consumed, have too much stew

indicators.note: only the final letter of goulash is taken
the letter is eaten, so it goes inside the eating

blocks.note: to overeat is to have too much

explanation.surface: A diner has finished the goulash and eaten too much stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stew' looks like more food alongside the goulash, but it is the verb, to get hot and bothered.
explanation.definitionFit: To stew is to be hot and flustered, which is to overheat.

clue.text: On the same page, I stay calm, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of calm counts

explanation.surface: Someone insisting they are in agreement and keeping their cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the same page' reads as the idiom for agreeing; the definition takes it literally, as in a footnote.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem (ibid.) is the Latin footnote term meaning in the same place, the same source or page just cited.

clue.text: Gold on key, little time for lead

blocks.note: Esc, the escape key on a keyboard
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A piece of kit described: gold fitted onto a key, and a little time to make the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Esc is the escape key on a computer keyboard; in an across clue 'on' means placed after.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to go with someone and show the way, as a guide or chaperone does.

clue.text: Less in order?

blocks.note: the surface reads 'fewer'; really the minus sign, subtraction in a child's words
the surface reads 'tidy'; really a meal you order in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Less' is the minus sign, take away in arithmetic; 'in order' is what you do with a takeaway, ordering food in.
explanation.definitionFit: A takeaway is a meal ordered from a restaurant to eat elsewhere, and 'take away' is the child's word for subtracting.

clue.text: 26 19's bottle-opener applied to thin bottle

indicators.note: the opener of bottle is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bottle-opener being used on a narrow bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' appears twice: first only its opening letter, then the whole word in its British sense of nerve. The answer runs on into 24 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe Spirit is Noel Coward's 1941 comedy about a novelist haunted by his first wife's ghost.

clue.text: Dog also has a pee when tickled

indicators.note: tickled letters squirm out of their places

blocks.note: pee is how the letter P is spelt out

explanation.surface: A dog that wets itself when tickled.
explanation.walkthrough: Pee is the letter P written as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lhasa apso is a small long-haired Tibetan breed of dog.

clue.text: See 22
Forecasters recalled problems in storms

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards

blocks.note: the Met Office, Britain's weather forecasters

explanation.surface: Weather forecasters called back to deal with trouble during storms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container indicator but here only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with a literary ring: the word for violent storms, as in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Dabbler teases swingers

blocks.note: a ham is an amateur, as in a ham radio operator

explanation.surface: An amateur flirting with people who swap partners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swingers' suggests partygoers; it is things that swing.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition by function: hanging beds sway, so the slang for partner-swapping couples is borrowed for them.

clue.text: Wind in low cloud slowing, mostly

indicators.note: most of the word, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: mist is cloud at ground level
rall., the musical direction rallentando, slowing down

explanation.surface: A weather report: wind in the low cloud is mostly dying down.
explanation.walkthrough: RALL is the score marking for rallentando; 'mostly' trims it to RAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The mistral is a strong cold wind blowing down the Rhône valley in southern France.

clue.text: Uncontaminated, set free over bug

indicators.note: set free, the letters of set move out of their order

blocks.note: to bug someone is to rile them

explanation.surface: A lab report: the sample is clean, and the insect has been released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set free' reads as one phrase meaning released; split, 'free' tells you to rearrange the word before it. In a down clue 'over' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile means free of germs, uncontaminated.

clue.text: See 26
Greeting witness heard?

indicators.note: heard means we go by the sound, not the spelling

explanation.surface: Someone called as a witness in court says hello.
explanation.walkthrough: In a London accent 'watcher' and 'wotcher' sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Wotcher is an informal Cockney greeting, like 'hello there', from 'what cheer'.

clue.text: Doctor of Literature endlessly circled by European ballerina

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter goes
the European forms a ring round the doctor

blocks.note: Dr Seuss, the children's author, a doctor in literature

explanation.surface: An academic, a doctor of letters, surrounded by a European dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor of Literature' reads as the degree D.Litt; it is Dr Seuss, a doctor who lives in literature.
explanation.definitionFit: A danseuse is a female ballet dancer.

clue.text: 26 19's tart?

blocks.note: a title from Noel Coward's work, his 1929 operetta
a tart may be sharp to taste yet is a sugary pastry

explanation.walkthrough: A tart can be sharp, bitter, or a sweet pastry; together they give a Coward title. The answer runs on into 3 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter Sweet is Noel Coward's 1929 operetta; bittersweet also describes something both sharp and sweet, like a tart.

clue.text: 26 19's fire once ignited in fictional schoolboy

indicators.note: set alight, the letters flare into a new arrangement
the rearranged letters go in the schoolboy

blocks.note: Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of the Greyfriars stories

explanation.surface: A fictional schoolboy's fire, lit once.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the fat schoolboy of Frank Richards's comic stories set at Greyfriars, a British boarding school. The answer runs on into 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief Encounter is the 1945 film of Noel Coward's play about a chance romance at a railway station.

clue.text: Knock out boxer as everyone gulps

indicators.note: the answer is swallowed inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A boxer scores a knockout and the whole crowd gasps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock out' and 'boxer' keep the surface in the ring, but the definition means delete.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock something out of a text or record is to erase it.

clue.text: See 12
Sovereign on flag, an individual from western Europe

blocks.note: a flag is a wild iris

explanation.surface: A monarch's portrait on a national flag, representing a European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner; it is the yellow flag, a wild waterside plant. In an across clue 'Sovereign on flag' puts the royal abbreviation second.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irishman is a man from Ireland, on Europe's western edge.

clue.text: Chicken expecting turkey, perhaps – to wit?

explanation.surface: A chicken nervously awaiting a turkey, as if at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse order: COWARD from 'Chicken', then NOEL from the time of year when a turkey is expected on the table.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward, playwright and composer, was famous for his wit.

clue.text: Once ref roughed up by Royal Engineers, impose rule again

indicators.note: roughed up, the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: RE = Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: A referee once beaten up by soldiers, then order is restored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' means beside here: RE joins the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-enforce is to enforce again, to impose a rule once more.
